history.title: Selection Week

data.body:
**Due:** (your teacher will tell you)

Most people can define natural selection and still explain it wrongly. This unit spends as much time on the wrong version as the right one, because the wrong version is the one that survives.

1. Read **Nothing Is Trying**. Mark every sentence that says what selection does *not* do.
2. Learn the words in **Selection Vocabulary**, then win the **Matching** game and the **Memory** game.
3. Work through **The Four Conditions** to see why the argument holds together.
4. Study the **Right Version, Wrong Version** chart.
5. Sort the cards in **How It Works or How It Doesn't?** — several are close.
6. Fill in **Selection Notes** as you read.
7. Take **Selection Check**.
8. Lock it in with **Remember the Four Conditions**.
9. Read **Questions People Ask About Evolution**.
10. Finish with **Investigation: Track the Trait**.

Bring one example of an organism that seems perfectly built for where it lives. 🧬

history.title: Nothing Is Trying
history.data:
## Nothing Is Trying

Here is a sentence you have probably heard: animals adapt to their environment. It sounds right. It is also the most common way of getting natural selection exactly backwards.

An individual does not adapt. **Populations** change across generations, and no individual in them changes at all.

### Four conditions, and that is the whole thing

Natural selection follows from four facts. If all four hold, it happens. There is nothing else to it.

**One: variation exists.** In any population, individuals differ. Some beetles are darker, some lighter. Some bacteria happen to carry a gene that a particular drug cannot disable. Crucially, **this variation is already there before the environment changes.** It was not requested and it was not produced on demand.

**Two: some of that variation is heritable.** Traits carried in genes get passed to offspring. Traits you acquire during your life do not. A weightlifter's children are not born strong, and a mouse that loses its tail has ordinary tailed pups.

**Three: more offspring are produced than can survive.** Food, space and safety run out. Not everyone makes it.

**Four: survival is not random with respect to those traits.** Some variants do better in this particular environment, so they leave more offspring.

Run those four for many generations and the **frequency** of a trait in the population shifts. That shift is the whole phenomenon.

### Why the wrong version is so appealing

The wrong version says an organism notices a problem and develops a solution. It is appealing because it is how *we* solve problems, and because the results genuinely look designed.

But nothing is trying. A **mutation** does not arrive because it would be useful. Mutations happen regardless, and most are neutral or harmful. Occasionally one turns out to help in the environment that happens to exist, and that one spreads — not because it was needed, but because its carriers left more offspring.

Bacteria make this concrete. Give a large population of bacteria an antibiotic and a few usually survive. Those few were not toughened by the drug. They already carried a variant that the drug could not disable, before it was ever applied. The antibiotic did not create resistance; it removed everything else. The next generation descends from the survivors, so more of it is resistant. Do that repeatedly and resistance becomes common.

This is also why antibiotics are worth using carefully rather than routinely, and why resistance is a serious medical problem rather than a textbook curiosity.

### Fit to what, exactly

**Fitness** in biology does not mean strong or fast. It means leaving more surviving offspring in this environment. A trait that helps in one place can be useless in another and harmful in a third.

So selection has no direction and no destination. Change the environment and the favoured trait can reverse within a few generations. Nothing is being perfected, because there is nothing to be perfect for.

What is left is simpler and stranger than the story people tell. Variation that already existed, filtered by conditions that happen to prevail, repeated until the population looks built for a world that merely selected it.

data.title: Remember the Four Conditions
data.instructions: Two cards carry what you will use on every example. Read the given one, build your own, then explain why yours works.
data.sourceExcerpt: The antibiotic did not create resistance; it removed everything else. The next generation descends from the survivors, so more of it is resistant.

cards.target: The four conditions, in the order they have to hold
essentialFacts: Variation exists, and it is already there beforehand.
Some of that variation is heritable.
More offspring are produced than can survive.
Survival is not random with respect to those traits.
cards.aiExample: Four beats: DIFFER, INHERIT, CROWD, FILTER. They differ. Some differences are inherited. There are too many of them. The environment filters. Say it in that order, because each beat is useless without the one before it.
cards.mapping: Four single words in a fixed order, and the order carries an argument: inheritance is pointless without variation, and filtering is pointless without crowding.
scaffoldSteps: Say the four beats out loud.
Run them on the antibiotic example.
Run them on an example of your own.
coachPrompts: Which of the four does your example not clearly show?
cards.studentPrompt: Build your own four-beat cue for the conditions.
cards.reasoningPrompt: What would happen if condition two failed but the other three held?

hookFact.text: If all four hold, it happens. There is nothing else to it.

cards.target: One question catches almost every wrong explanation
essentialFacts: Individuals do not change; populations do.
Only the proportions of variants shift.
If your explanation has an individual changing, it is the wrong version.
cards.aiExample: Picture a jar of red and blue marbles. Selection never repaints a marble. It only removes marbles, and the jar afterwards is a different mix of exactly the same marbles. If your explanation repaints anything, it is wrong.
cards.mapping: Repainting is a vivid, specific thing to watch for, and it is precisely the move the wrong version makes. Removal versus repainting is the entire distinction in one image.
cards.scaffoldStarter: In my explanation, did anything get repainted? ____. Instead, what changed was ____.
scaffoldSteps: Underline every verb attached to a single organism.
Ask whether any of them repaints a marble.
coachPrompts: Point at the individual in your sentence. Did it change?
cards.studentPrompt: Make your own image for removal rather than repainting.
cards.reasoningPrompt: Why does the repainting version feel so much more natural to say?

history.title: Selection Check

questions.question: What actually changes when a population undergoes natural selection?
options: The proportion of individuals carrying a trait changes
Each individual gradually adjusts its own body over its lifetime
Every member of the species develops the useful trait at once
The environment changes to suit the species living in it
questions.correctAnswer: The proportion of individuals carrying a trait changes

questions.question: When does the variation that selection acts on arise?
options: It is produced in response to the new conditions
It is already present before the environment changes
It appears only once the old variants have died out
It is created by the environment acting on the parents
questions.correctAnswer: It is already present before the environment changes

questions.question: A weightlifter builds a great deal of muscle. What do their children inherit?
options: More muscle than average, since the parent developed it
Slightly more muscle, but only in the first generation
Nothing from that training, because it is an acquired trait
The muscle itself, but not the ability to maintain it
questions.correctAnswer: Nothing from that training, because it is an acquired trait

questions.question: A few bacteria survive a course of antibiotics. What does this show?
options: The drug toughened those particular bacteria up
Those bacteria learned to withstand the drug over time
The drug caused a helpful mutation in the survivors
Those bacteria already carried a variant the drug could not disable
questions.correctAnswer: Those bacteria already carried a variant the drug could not disable

questions.question: In biology, what does fitness mean?
options: Leaving more surviving offspring in this environment
Being the strongest member of the population
Being physically healthy and free of disease
Being able to survive in the widest range of places
questions.correctAnswer: Leaving more surviving offspring in this environment

questions.question: Why does natural selection have no direction or destination?
options: Because it works far too slowly to have any pattern
Because what counts as helpful depends on current conditions
Because mutations occur at a completely steady rate
Because every trait is equally useful in every environment
questions.correctAnswer: Because what counts as helpful depends on current conditions

questions.question: Most mutations are best described as which of the following?
options: Helpful, which is why species keep improving
Always harmful, since any change breaks something
Neutral or harmful, with helpful ones being uncommon
Produced deliberately when an organism needs them
questions.correctAnswer: Neutral or harmful, with helpful ones being uncommon

questions.question: Rewrite this sentence so it is accurate: "Over time, the moths turned darker so they could hide against the sooty trees."
questions.expectedAnswer: Darker and lighter moths were both already present in the population. Against sooty trees the darker ones were harder for predators to see, so they survived and reproduced more often. Over generations the proportion of dark moths in the population increased. No moth changed colour, and none of it happened so that anything could hide.

questions.question: Explain why saying "a species develops a trait because it needs it" gets the mechanism backwards.
questions.expectedAnswer: Need does not produce variation. Mutations happen regardless of whether they would be useful, and most are neutral or harmful. A trait spreads only if it happens to already exist and happens to help its carriers leave more offspring in the environment that happens to prevail. The usefulness follows from the spread rather than causing it.

history.title: Questions People Ask About Evolution

data.question: If most mutations are harmful, how does anything ever improve? 🧬
data.answer: Because harmful ones are removed and the rare helpful one spreads. Populations are large and generations are many, so even a very uncommon helpful variant gets its chance. The filter does the work, not the mutation rate.

data.question: Does natural selection explain everything about how species change?
data.answer: No, and biologists are clear about that. Random genetic drift changes small populations by chance alone, and some traits are carried along simply because they sit near a useful gene. Selection is the main mechanism behind traits that look well-suited, not the only thing happening.

data.question: Are humans still evolving? 🌍
data.answer: Yes. Lactose tolerance in adults spread in populations with a long history of dairy farming, and it is a well-studied recent example. Evolution does not stop; it just happens on a timescale longer than a lifetime.

data.question: Is the phrase survival of the fittest wrong? 🤔
data.answer: It is not wrong so much as badly worded for modern ears. Fittest meant best-fitting to the conditions, not strongest. Because the everyday meaning of fit has drifted, most biologists avoid the phrase entirely.

data.question: Why do some organisms look so perfectly designed? 🐦
data.answer: Because you are seeing the survivors of an enormous filter, and not the countless variants that failed. Looked at closely, organisms are full of awkward compromises, which is what you would expect from something assembled by filtering rather than planning.

data.question: Can a trait become common without being useful at all?
data.answer: It can. In a small population, chance alone can make a neutral trait common, which is genetic drift. Usefulness makes spreading much more likely, but it is not the only route.

data.question: Why does antibiotic resistance matter so much? 💊
data.answer: Because we are running the experiment constantly and at scale. Every use of an antibiotic removes susceptible bacteria and leaves resistant ones to reproduce. That is why doctors avoid prescribing them when they will not help, and why you should follow the instructions you were actually given rather than a rule of thumb you half remember.

history.title: Investigation: Track the Trait
history.meta: 8th Grade • Investigation brief • model a frequency shift, then audit your own language

data.title: Track the Trait
data.instructions: Model several generations of selection with counters, record how the trait frequency changes, and then audit your own written explanation for the wrong version.
data.fitReason: The frequency shift is the whole phenomenon and students almost never see one happen. Running it by hand makes the population the thing that changes, and the language audit at the end is where most students discover they have written the wrong version without noticing.

brief.context: You will have a bag of counters in two colours standing for two variants of one heritable trait, plus a rule your teacher gives you for which colour survives in this environment. You may change the environment rule partway through if you say when you did it.
brief.audience: The class, who will compare frequency graphs and hunt each other's write-ups for the wrong version
brief.drivingQuestion: What exactly is it that changes from one generation to the next?
brief.seedDirection: Record the starting counts before you touch anything. Without generation zero you have nothing to compare against.
lockedLessonFacts: Variation is already present before the environment changes.
Only heritable traits can be selected; acquired traits cannot.
More offspring are produced than can survive.
The frequency of a trait in the population shifts, while no individual changes.
openQuestions: How many generations before the change was obvious?
Did the disfavoured variant disappear completely, and does that matter?
What happened when the environment rule reversed?
stakeholders: Your partner, who is checking your counts
The class, who will read your explanation critically
A student next year who will read the wrong version somewhere and need this
criteria: Starting frequencies recorded before generation one
At least six generations, with counts for each
A graph of the trait frequency across generations
A written explanation with no sentence in which an individual changes
One sentence saying what your model does not represent well
constraints: The environment rule must be fixed in advance and stated, and any change to it recorded
Report every generation, including any that went against the trend
Under one page of writing, plus your table and graph
You may not write that an organism adapts, tries, wants or needs anything
brief.deliverable: A one-page report with your table, your frequency graph, an explanation that survives the language audit, and one sentence on what the counter model fails to capture.

parallelExample.context: A pair ran six generations and their dark counters went from a quarter of the bag to nearly three quarters.
parallelExample.move: Their first write-up said the population adapted to the new conditions. Running the language audit, they underlined adapted and found it was doing the work of a whole explanation. They rewrote it as a statement about which counters were removed each round and what that did to the proportions, and the sentence got longer and much better.
parallelExample.whyItHelps: The banned words are not a style rule. Each of them hides the mechanism, and being forced around them makes a student state the mechanism out loud.

supports.frameStarter: At generation zero, ____ per cent carried ____. By generation six, ____. This happened because ____.
frameChoices: Model a predator that spots one colour more easily
Model a drug that one variant survives
Model a food source only one variant can reach
Model an environment that reverses partway through
coachPrompts: What did you record before generation one?
Is there a sentence where a single organism changes? Rewrite it.
Did any counter change colour at any point? What does that tell you?
What does the bag of counters fail to represent about a real population?
